summary.text: The North Atlantic Oscillation is the rise and fall of the sea-level pressure difference between the Icelandic Low and the Azores High.
By changing the strength of those two pressure systems, it sets how hard and in which direction westerly winds blow and where storms travel across the North Atlantic.
A large pressure gap brings mild, wet winters to Central Europe, while a small one leaves northern Europe cold and dry and sends storms toward the Mediterranean.

facts.label: Two pressure centers
facts.value: The Icelandic Low and the Azores High

facts.label: Discovered
facts.value: Through studies in the late 1800s and early 1900s

facts.label: Sea level effect
facts.value: Millibars of pressure change move sea level by centimeters

facts.value: The Arctic oscillation, or Northern Annular Mode

items.prompt: This winter the pressure gap between Iceland and the Azores is unusually large. What kind of winter should someone in Germany expect?

options.label: Bitterly cold and very dry
Hot, with frequent heat waves
Mild, with frequent rain
Calm, with almost no wind

items.explain: A high index strengthens the westerlies, which bring mild and wet winters to Central Europe.

items.prompt: In a low-index winter, northern Europe turns cold and dry. Where do the storms that would have soaked it tend to go instead?

options.label: South, toward southern Europe and North Africa
North, into the high Arctic and Greenland
West, onto the coast of California
Nowhere; the storms simply stop forming

items.explain: With the westerlies suppressed, storms track south toward the Mediterranean, bringing more storms and rain to southern Europe and North Africa.

items.prompt: During a positive phase, air pressure over a stretch of coast falls a few millibars. What happens to the sea level there?

options.label: It drops by several meters
It stays exactly the same
It drops by a few centimeters
It rises by a few centimeters

items.explain: Lower air pressure lets the sea surface rise, the inverse barometer effect, and pressure swings of millibars shift sea level by centimeters.

items.prompt: El Niño in the Pacific is driven heavily by the ocean. What mostly drives the North Atlantic Oscillation?

options.label: Slow shifts in deep ocean currents
Changes in the air above the ocean
The 11-year cycle of sunspots
Melting and freezing of sea ice

items.explain: Unlike El Niño–Southern Oscillation, the NAO is a largely atmospheric mode, a swing in air pressure between two weather systems.

items.prompt: One season the Azores High sits farther south than usual. Where are major Atlantic hurricanes more likely to be pushed?

options.label: Up the North American Atlantic coast
Straight across to western Europe
Into the Gulf of Mexico
North toward Iceland

items.explain: A southern Azores High tends to force storms into the Gulf of Mexico, while a northern position lets them track up the Atlantic coast.

items.prompt: A strongly positive phase warms the North Sea, where young cod already live near the top of the temperatures they can stand. What happens to them?

options.label: They grow faster and more survive
Nothing, since fish ignore water temperature
They move into the Labrador Sea to breed
Fewer of the cod larvae survive

items.explain: The NAO+ warming of the North Sea reduces survival of cod larvae there, because they are at the upper limits of their temperature tolerance.

paragraphs.heading: Two pressure centres
paragraphs.text: The North Atlantic Oscillation, or NAO, is a swing in the difference in sea-level air pressure between two big weather systems. One is the Icelandic Low, a permanent low-pressure system over Iceland; the other is the Azores High, a permanent high-pressure system over the Azores. How strong these two are, and where they sit, changes from year to year, and that variation is what the name describes. Through those changes, the NAO sets how hard and in which direction the westerly winds blow, and where storms travel across the North Atlantic.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: The NAO is one of the most important ways climate fluctuates in the North Atlantic and the humid lands around it. Unlike El Niño in the Pacific, it is largely a pattern in the atmosphere. Several studies in the late 1800s and early 1900s brought it to light. Above all from November to April, it drives much of the changing weather in the region: wind speed and direction, temperature, moisture, and the number, strength and paths of storms. It is a close relative of the Arctic oscillation, but a different thing from the Atlantic multidecadal oscillation.

paragraphs.heading: High index, low index
paragraphs.text: Westerly winds carry moist air from the Atlantic into Europe. When the pressure gap between the Icelandic Low and the Azores High is large, called a high index or NAO+, the westerlies strengthen. Central Europe and its Atlantic coast then get cool summers and mild, wet winters. When the index is low, or NAO−, the westerlies weaken, northern Europe has cold, dry winters, and storms head south toward the Mediterranean Sea, bringing more storms and rain to southern Europe and North Africa.

paragraphs.heading: Across the Atlantic
paragraphs.text: Most agree its effect on the United States is much smaller than on western Europe, but it is still thought to reach much of the upper central and eastern parts of North America. In a high-index winter, the Azores High pulls a stronger south-westerly flow over the eastern half of the continent, which stops Arctic air plunging into the United States south of 40° latitude. In a low-index winter, the upper central and north-eastern United States can get more cold outbreaks than usual, with heavy snowstorms. Where the Azores High sits also steers major hurricanes: a southern position tends to drive them into the Gulf of Mexico, while a northern one lets them run up the Atlantic coast of North America.

paragraphs.heading: Sea level and fish
paragraphs.text: The pattern even reaches sea level and fisheries. Under NAO+, lower air pressure over a region raises the sea there, through the inverse barometer effect; pressure swings measured in millibars can shift sea level by centimeters. NAO+ also warms the North Sea and cools the Labrador Sea, and both cut the survival of cod larvae, which in each sea live near the edge of the temperatures they can bear. The NAO+ peak of the early 1990s may have played a part, though not the deciding one, in the collapse of the Newfoundland cod fishery.

paragraphs.heading: Sheep and grasshoppers
paragraphs.text: Its reach on land can be unexpected. The strength of the NAO helps decide how numbers of Soay sheep rise and fall. On the tall-grass prairies of the US Midwest, where the NAO does not change the weather much, Jonas and Joern found in 2007 that common grasshopper species grew more abundant after winters in the positive phase. Less common species, by contrast, did better after winters in the negative phase.
